NATURE
OF THE APPLICATION

[
1
]

The applicant, James Edward Kopec, as
executor of the Estate of Violet Delrose Moore, has made an application to vary
the trust created by the Last Will and Testament of the deceased in order to
increase the amount allocated annually from the income of the trust to charitable
purposes, namely, a monthly stipend of $500.00 to the Weyburn Humane Society
and two annual scholarships for students in the amount of $500.00 each. The
applicant proposes to increase the payment to the Weyburn Humane Society to $2,000.00
per month, and to increase the scholarships amounts to $2,000.00 each.

BACKGROUND FACTS

[
2
]

Violet Delrose Moore died on February 2,
2010, at the age of 91 years. By her Last Will and Testament made on December
31, 1997, she appointed the applicant, James Edward Kopec, as sole executor of
her estate. The will instructs her executor to pay her liabilities, including
testamentary and funeral expenses, and her taxes, from her general estate.
Household and personal effects were to be dealt with as follows:

2.(b)
Household Goods and Personal Effects:
My Estate
Trustee shall distribute the following of my household and personal effects as
follows:

My
household and personal effects shall be held in trust by my Estate Trustee,
these effects can be sold at such time should my estate become depleted and
finances are needed to continue my cash gift bequest.

[
3
]

The Will thereafter instructs the
executor to make cash gifts in the following terms:

2.(c)
Cash and Specific Gifts:
My Estate Trustee shall pay cash gifts
as follows:

$500.00
each month

shall be given to the Weyburn Humane Society to aid in the care for its pets.
This money is to be used for food for the pets, Weyburn Humane Society building
upkeep, veterinary services, heat and or power for the Weyburn Humane Society
building. My Estate Trustee shall insure (sic) these conditions are being met,
or money shall be withheld until conditions are met.

$500.00
each year
shall
be designated toward an English Scholarship though Weyburn Comprehensive School. English Scholarship shall be given in my name.

$500.00
each year

shall be designated to an under privileged student to attend a college or
university. Student shall be chosen by my Estate Trustee.

[
4
]

The deceased also owned farm land,
interests in oil well surface leases, and mineral rights for which she gave the
following specific instructions:

2.(d)
Real Estate:
My Estate Trustee shall deal with my real estate as
follows:

My
farmland

(SE and SW quarters of Section 27, Township 5, Range 14, West of the Second
Meridian) and (SE and SW quarters of Section 23, Township 5, Range 14, West of
the Second Meridian) shall be left to my general estate, moneys from its rental
shall be used for its improvements or debts incurred by the farmland and moneys
from its rental shall also be used to support my specific gift request.

All
of my presently owned oil leases, surface rights, mineral rights, LeClare
Trailer Park payments, Crocus Motel property (Lot 1 to 6 inclusive, Block 218,
Plan T-1166 West Hill in the City of Weyburn), 224-3
rd
St. (Lot N ½
of 8, Block 22, Plan 31899 in the City of Weyburn) shall be left to general
estate for my Estate Trustee to deal with. He shall finalize all dealings for
the best dollar value and do what he must to insure (sic) money shall be
available to carry out my specific gift request as long as possible.

[
5
]

The Will contains another provision
under the heading of “Residue” which does not make a separate gift of the rest
and residue as one would normally expect but instead simply provides instructions
to apply any assets which may be discovered later toward fulfilment of the
specific bequests previously made. It reads:

2.(e)
Residue:

My Estate Trustee shall pay or transfer all of the remainder of my estate (“the
residue”) as follows: If presently undiscovered properties, i.e.: personal
effects, debts owed to me, unknown mineral rights, are discovered by my Estate
Trustee, they shall be added to my general estate for my Estate Trustee to use
to insure (sic) my specific gifts requests are continued.

[
6
]

The Will grants broad power and
discretion to the executor to administer the estate as a going concern. Clause
3 of the Will provides as follows:

3.
Administrative and Trust Provisions:
The following
administrative and trust provisions shall, if relevant, apply to the terms of
this Will:

(a)

Estate
Trustee Powers:
My Estate Trustee shall have all of the available
powers, as and when necessary, to properly and efficiently administer my
estate, including power to: sell my property for cash if and when necessary; or
postpone such sale; invest my property in any type of investment whatsoever
until disposed of; manage, maintain, repair, and improve my property; settle
claims and debts; carry on any business; make income tax elections; borrow,
lend, and lease; and be reimbursed and remunerated for undertaking such office.

(b)

Community
of Property:
No gift under this Will, nor any future income,
profits, and appreciation realized by such gift, shall constitute “net family
property,” nor be part of and “community of property” as between any
beneficiary and his or her consort.

The latter “Community of Property” clause is, of
course, superfluous in that no gift of property is made to any named
individual. The only beneficiaries are the Weyburn Humane Society and two
students whose identities are unknown until chosen each year, one by the Weyburn Comprehensive School and the other by the executor. This clause might be relevant,
however, if part of the estate is deemed to have passed on an intestacy.

[
7
]

The Statement of Property filed with the
application for probate indicated that the value of the property located in Saskatchewan was $415,720.53, with an additional interest in land in Manitoba valued at

[
8
]

The executor, Mr. Kopec, filed the
application for probate on November 2, 2010. Upon reviewing the application,
this Court noted immediately that the capital and potential income which could
be generated from the capital would far exceed the total annual commitment of
$7,000.00 payable to the three named “charities”, namely, the Weyburn Humane
Society, the English scholarship and the underprivileged student scholarship.
This court therefore inquired of the solicitor for the executor, Mr. Scott
Moffat, whether it was the executor’s intention to apply for variation of the
will to deal with this “accumulations” situation.

[
9
]

In a telephone conference a few days
later, Mr. Moffat advised this Court that he was well apprised of the fact that
the income stream in this estate was likely to exceed the annual commitments to
the named charities resulting in accumulation of income in perpetuity. He advised
that the executor may eventually apply to the court for directions with regard
to the excess income, such as increasing the payment to the named charities or
similar charities so that the deceased’s intentions could be carried out as
near as possible to the intentions included in the Will. This Court suggested
to Mr. Moffat that other outcomes were also possible, such as a declaration of
intestacy in respect of the accumulated income that was not required to satisfy
the annual commitments to the named charities and the cost of administering the
estate.

[
10
]

On November 30, 2010, this Court ordered
that letters probate should issue to the applicant but also ordered that he
must report to this Court on a periodic basis with regard to the administration
of the estate. The executor was asked to file his first report within six
months of the grant of probate and every six months thereafter unless otherwise
directed by a judge of this Court. The report was to inform the court what
assets had been taken into administration, what debts had been paid, and what
the anticipated annual income would be. An estimate of the costs of
administering the estate was also to be included. Additionally, the executor
was to inform the court who the beneficiaries would be in the event that an
intestacy existed in respect of any part of this estate.

[
11
]

The first report filed by the executor
on June 7, 2011, indicated that in the period from the date of death on
February 2, 2010, to May 26, 2011, the estate had received income from dividends,
interest, land rent, royalties, water disposal and surface leases totalling
$88,566.29. This total did not include non-recurring income such as the last
Canada Pension Plan cheque in the amount of $308.38. In that same period, the
executor paid expenses such as accounting fees, bank charges, funeral expenses,
income taxes, legal fees, property taxes and other testamentary debts totalling
$108,285.12. Included in that total was $78,498.82 paid to Revenue Canada for income taxes, most of which was presumably non-recurring.

[
12
]

In the second report filed on December
7, 2011, the executor reported that there was $188,715.12 in the bank account
and that he continued to administer the land and mineral interests. Excluding
the specific commitments for the Humane Society and Scholarships, the amount
paid for taxes and estate administration in the five previous months was
$2,840.57. The executor estimated that the annual income, based on a two-year
average, would be $58,034.10. He also estimated that income taxes would be
$17,000.00 per year and that administration costs, including accounting, legal
and executor fees, would be approximately $7,419.44. This would result in
annual net income of $33,614.66, of which only $7,000.00 is required to cover
the charitable bequests. The surplus would be approximately $26,614.66 per
year.

[
13
]

In the second report, Mr. Moffat
informed the court that he was uncertain who would be the beneficiaries
entitled to share in the estate in the event any portion would pass under an
intestacy. Mr. Moffat did indicate, however, that someone in Ontario had
claimed on an earlier matter to be a cousin of the deceased.

[
14
]

In the second report, Mr. Moffat also
indicated that the executor would soon be applying to triple the amount paid to
the three named charities. The current application actually requests permission
to increase the amount of the charitable bequests to the Humane Society and the
scholarships by four times the amount specified in the Last Will and Testament.

THE LAW

[
15
]

There are a number of legal issues which
arise as a result of the testamentary dispositions made in the Last Will and
Testament of the deceased, Violet Delrose Moore. In addition to the probability
of accumulation of income there is also the matter that the corpus of the estate,
including the interests in land, will never vest in any individual or
corporation other than the executor. It appears that the estate will run in
perpetuity. It will never end. The executor will be responsible to administer
the trust property during the whole of his lifetime, and the responsibility to
continue to administer it will fall to his executor and thereafter to that
executor’s executor, and so on and so on.

[
16
]

Historically, the issue of testators
writing wills which fail to eventually cede control and ownership of land and
personal property within a reasonable time was dealt with by application of
“the rule against perpetuities”. It may be useful at this juncture to explain
what that rule is.

[
17
]

In

Irving Industries (Irvine Wireline Products Division) Ltd. v. Canadian
Long Island Petroleums Ltd.,
1974 CanLII 190 (SCC)
,
[1975] 2 S.C.R. 715
,
[1974] S.C.J. No. 122 (QL
)
, at page 11,
the
Supreme Court of Canada used the following quote to explain the rule against
perpetuities:

In
considering the application of the rule against perpetuities in the
circumstances of the present case it is useful to consider its background. The
history of the rule is outlined in Cheshire’s Modern Real Property, 10th ed.,
at pp. 234 and 235, as follows:

The
history of the rules whereby settlors have been prevented from limiting remote
interests, is the history of a conflict between two antagonistic ideas. On the
one hand there is the desire of the man of means to regulate the future
enjoyment of his property for as long a period as possible. The right of making
a settlement or a will is a potent weapon in the hands of a declining man, and
unless human nature is transformed, the opportunity it offers of fixing the pecuniary
destinies of the coming generations will not be neglected. A landowner, unless
he gives thought to the fiscal consequences, is not always content to leave a
large estate at the free disposal of a son. Old age especially, satisfied with
its own achievements and often irritated by the apparent follies of a
degenerate time, is inclined to restrain each generation of beneficiaries
within close limits, and to provide for a series of limited interests. A
landowner views the free power of alienation with complacency when it resides
in his own hand, but he does not feel the same equanimity with regard to its
transfer to others.

“But
the freedom of alienation and devise was not congenial to the spirit in which
great landowners viewed their land. To preserve their family name and position,
‘to keep the land in the family,’ seemed to them a desirable and even laudable
object, to restrain any individual holder of the land from dealing with it so
as to interfere with the interest of subsequent generations of the family in
the family land was a necessary means to this end. To contrive restraints on
alienation and succession which the law would enforce, to ascertain the
furthest limits up to which the law would allow the grasp of the dead hand to
be kept on the hand of the living, was the task set by the great landowners
before their legal advisers.” (Scrutton, Land in Fetters, p. 108.)

This
aspiration, however, soon aroused the antagonism of the courts. The law is
moved, and from the earliest times always has been moved, by a deep-seated
antipathy to this human love of power. It is one thing to permit the free power
of alienation, another to allow it to be exercised to its own destruction. The
view of the law is that no disposition should be allowed which tends to
withdraw land from commerce, and in pursuance of this policy two rules have
emerged which have successfully prevented the particular evil of “perpetuities,”
though they are essentially different from each other in nature. The first,
directed against inalienable interests and often called the old rule against
perpetuities, forbids the creation of any form of unbarrable entail; the
second, the modern rule against perpetuities, invalidates an interest that may
vest at too remote a date in the future.

The
perpetuity period is defined by Cheshire at p. 240:

At common law,
the vesting of an interest may be postponed during the lives of persons in
being at the time when the instrument of creation takes effect, plus a further
period of twenty-one years after the extinction of the last life. Any interest
so limited that it may possibly vest after the expiration of this period is
totally void.

[
18
]

The rule against perpetuities is not a
statutory provision, but was created judicially. However, with the adoption of
The

Trustee Act, 2009
, S.S. 2009, c. T-23.01 (effective January 1, 2010) and
specifically s. 58 thereof, the rules against perpetuities are no longer the
law of Saskatchewan. In this context, the statute defines “rules against
perpetuities” as both the modern rules against perpetuities, defined in s. 57
as “the operation of the rule with regard to remoteness of vesting and
perpetual duration and with regard to testamentary executor interests in
personalty” and “the rule in
Whitby v. Mitchell
”. This latter rule
refers to the prohibition against a settlement of lands to unborn persons of
yet unborn persons, explained in the following passage from
Phillips (Re)

(1913),
1913 CanLII 510 (ON SCHCD)
,
11 D.L.R. 500
,
[1913] O.J. No. 37 (QL)
at para.
18
:

18
In
Whitby
v. Mitchell

(1889),
42 Ch. D. 494
, Kay, J., had before him a case in which
the lands were, by settlement, limited to the use of the husband and wife for
life, with remainder to the use of their issue (born before any appointment) as
they should by deed appoint. They appointed part of the lands to the use of the
daughter for life, and after her death to the use of such person as she should
by will appoint, and, in default of appointment, to her children. It was held
that the only part of the appointment which was good was the gift to the
daughter. The learned Judge says, referring to various unsuccessful attempts to
tie up land: “One of the things attempted has been to make successive
limitations of life interests to unborn persons and to the children of those
unborn persons. That has always been treated as being an invalid limitation of
real estate. You may limit for life to an unborn person; but you cannot limit
it for life to the unborn person so as to tie it up until the death of that
unborn person --that is to say, any remainder limited after the life estate
must be to a person in esse at the time that it was made.” This rule is said to
be an absolute rule, independent of the rule against perpetuities, and of
feudal origin. This case was affirmed in
(1890),
44 Ch.D. 85
.

[
19
]

It is also of consequence in this case
that
The
Trustee Act, 2009
, more specifically
s. 59
, also repealed
the
Accumulations Act
. The
Accumulations Act
is defined in s. 57
as the Act of Great Britain, being chapter 98 of 39 & 40 George III, known
as the
Accumulations Act, 1800
. The fact that the
Accumulations Act,
1800
applied in Saskatchewan and what it proscribed was noted
in
this passage from
Hume Estate (Re)
,
1983 CanLII 2489 (SK SU)
,
[1983] 4 W.W.R. 728
,
[1983] S.J. No.
293 (QL)
at para.
7
:

7
i) There
would appear to be no doubt that The Accumulation Act, 39 and 40 Geo. III, c.
98 applies in the province of Saskatchewan. (Re Fossum Estate
(1960)
1960 CanLII 189 (SK QB)
,
32 W.W.R.
372
). That act provides that no person shall ... by any will, codicil or
otherwise howsoever), settle or dispose of any real or personal property in
such manner that the rents and profits therefrom shall be accumulated for a
term longer than the life of the grantor or the term of 21 years from the
testator. There are other periods of time mentioned in the statute but they are
not material to this matter. In every case where there is direction to
accumulate beyond the period of time, such direction is null and void.

[
20
]

Presumably the reason for abrogating
both the rules against perpetuities and the
Accumulations Act, 1800,
was
to mitigate the harsh effects which could occur when provisions of wills or
trusts are declared to be “null and void” because of breach of these historical
and somewhat archaic rules. However, that does not mean that the public policy
which led to the creation of these rules or ordinances was necessarily wrong or
misplaced. In fact, the legislature recognized that there may still be
situations where dispositions formerly subject to the rules against
perpetuities or accumulations should be reviewed for their propriety. In this
regard,
ss. 51(1)
of
The
Trustee Act, 2009
,
provides as follows:

51(1)
If a will, trust, settlement or other disposition creates an interest in property
that might be void if the rules against perpetuities or the Accumulations Act
were still part of the law of Saskatchewan, the court, on the application of an
interested party, may maintain, vary or terminate that interest on any terms
that the court considers appropriate.

[
21
]

This authority of the court to approve
variations of dispositions formerly subject to the rules against perpetuities
and accumulations stems from the general authority granted to the courts under

s. 49
of
The
Trustee Act, 2009
, which states as follows:

49(1)
In this section, “
person
” includes an association of persons.

(2)
If property is held on trusts arising before, on or after the coming into force
of this Part under any will, trust, settlement or other disposition, the court
may, on the application of any interested party, make an order on behalf of a
person mentioned in subsection (4):

(a)

varying or revoking all or any of the
trusts; or

(b)

enlarging
the powers of the trustee with respect to managing or administering any of the
property subject to the trusts.

(3)
An interested party making an application pursuant to this section shall serve a
copy of the application on the Public Guardian and Trustee.

(4) The court may make an order pursuant to
subsection (2) on behalf of:

(a)
any person having an interest, whether vested or contingent, under the trusts
who by reason of being a minor or other incapacity is incapable of assenting;

(b)
any person, whether ascertained or not, who may become entitled to an interest
under the trusts at a future date or on the happening of a future event;

(c)
any person unborn; or

(d)
any person with respect to any interest of that person that may arise by reason
of any discretionary power given to anyone on the failure or determination of
any existing interest that has not failed or determined.

(5)
The court may make an order pursuant to this section whether or not there is any
other person beneficially interested who is capable of assenting to the arrangement.

(6)
The court shall not approve an arrangement on behalf of any person coming within
clause (4)(a), (b) or (c) unless the carrying out of the arrangement appears to
be for the benefit of that person.

[
22
]

Section 50
of
The
Trustee Act, 2009
,

specifically addresses the authority of the Courts to review trusts for
charitable or non-charitable purposes. It states as follows:

50(1)
If property is held on trusts arising before, on or after the coming into force
of this Part under any will, trust, settlement or other disposition, the court
may, on the application of any interested party, make an order on behalf of a
charitable or non-charitable purpose that is the subject of the trusts:

(a)
varying or revoking all or any of the trusts;

(b)
enlarging the powers of the trustee with respect to managing or administering
any of the property subject to the trusts;

(c)
merging all or any of the trusts with another trust; or

(d)
resettling any interest under the trust.

(2)
The court may make an order pursuant to this section whether or not there is
any other person beneficially interested who is capable of assenting to the
arrangement.

(3)
The court shall not approve an arrangement unless it is satisfied that in all
the circumstances at the time of the application to the court the arrangement
appears to be of a justifiable character.

[
23
]

There is one other legal principle that
I wish to discuss before dealing with the merits of the current application to
quadruple the annual bequests to the specified charities.

[
24
]

In the brief filed on the within application,
Mr. Moffat suggests that this Court should apply what is known as the
cy-pres

doctrine. The
cy-pres
doctrine is an equitable doctrine which allows
a court to amend, re-write or interpret a written instrument such as a
will
that contains a gift to a charity to implement as near as possible the donor’s
intent and to prevent the failure of the gift.
In
Robbins
Estate (Re)
,
1974 CanLII 950 (SK QB)
,
[1974] 6 W.W.R. 635
,
[1974] S.J. No. 201(QL)
(Sask. Q.B.) at
para.
5
, Hughes J. referred to
Re MacAulay; Bd. of Governors of Dunstan University v. University of P.E.I.
(1971)
,
1971 CanLII 1127 (PE SCTD)
,
18 D.L.R. (3d) 726
,
[1971] P.E.I.J. No.
51(QL)
where Tweedy J. stated:

In
my opinion a concise definition of the
cy-près
doctrine would be where a
clear charitable intention is expressed, it will not be permitted to fail
because of the mode, if specified cannot be executed, but the law will
substitute another mode,
cy-pres
, that is as near as possible to the
mode specified by the donor.'

[
25
]

This doctrine is resorted to, for
example, where a bequest is made to a non-existent institution and the court
must decide whether it was the testator’s intention to make a general
charitable gift or a gift to a particular charity.

[
26
]

In his brief, Mr. Moffat refers to the
case of
Jewish Home for the Aged of British Columbia v. Toronto General
Trusts Corp.
,
1961 CanLII 295 (SCC)
,
[1961] S.C.R. 465
,
[1961] S.C.J. No. 24(QL)
, for the
proposition that the
cy-pres
doctrine could be used to determine how
surplus income should be allocated, especially as between the charitable
objects and those who would take under intestacy. In that case, the testator
left
his property in trust to a corporate trustee. After making provision for
certain bequests, he directed the accumulation out of residuary income of three
funds, each of $20,000.00, the first for a Jewish hospital, the second for a
Jewish orphan asylum and the third for a Jewish old men’s home. No such
institutions were in existence at the date of the testator’s death. Fourteen
years after his death, an institution which fit the description of “a Jewish
old men’s home” came into existence and claimed the fund and one third of the
residue. The Supreme Court of Canada decided that the institution fitting the
charitable purpose had come into existence within the perpetuity period. The court
also decided that monies must not be accumulated after 21 years following the
testator’s death, and then made the following decision in respect of the
surplus income thereafter:

The
next question is the destination of the surplus income after July 5, 1957. All
that has happened here is that the testator has directed an accumulation to
extend beyond the legal limit in the carrying out of a general charitable
intention. In these circumstances, the surplus income does not go to the
next-of-kin but is to be applied cy-près. This was the result in
Re Monk
[
[1927]
2 Ch. 197
,
96 L.J. Ch. 296
.], and in
Re Bradwell's Will Trusts
[
[1952] 2
All E.R. 286
,
[1952] Ch. 575
.]. The rule is stated in Gray, 4th ed., at p. 630,
as follows:

But
where there is an unconditional gift to charity, the gift will be regarded as
immediate and good, although the particular mode of carrying out the charity
which the donor has indicated is too remote. Consequently in such a case if a
direction for accumulation is invalid the only result is that the income is
immediately distributable in charity; the heirs or next of kin are not let in.

The same
principle is stated in 4 Hals., 3rd ed., 319. I notice a recent application of
it in
Re Burns Estate
[
(1960),
1960 CanLII 277 (AB SCAD)
,
32 W.W.R. 689
,
25 D.L.R. (2d) 427
.] [Alberta Sup. Court, App. Div.] A scheme must therefore be settled by the Court for the
cy-près

application of all the surplus income after July 5, 1957.

[
27
]

Mr. Moffat argues that in circumstances
such as exist in this case, the excess funds should be paid out proportionately
in fulfilment of the charitable purposes described in the will, namely, for the
purposes of the Weyburn Humane Society, for an English scholarship to a student
attending Weyburn Comprehensive School, and for a scholarship to an
underprivileged student chosen by the executor to attend a college or
university. Mr. Moffat advises that Weyburn Humane Society, Weyburn Comprehensive School and the executor all agree that it would be fair and equitable
that they should proportionately share the excess income which would otherwise
simply accumulate. They take the position that the class of beneficiary is
closed and that it would be contrary to the deceased’s intention to let in any
heirs or next of kin.

THE ISSUE

[
28
]

The issue before me is whether I should
allow for the quadrupling of the amount payable to the named “charities”
mentioned in the will of Violet Delrose Moore as a means of dealing with the
accumulation of income in amounts which presently far exceed what is required
to meet the annual obligations of the testamentary trust.

[
29
]

For the reasons which follow, I am of
the opinion that the present application should be adjourned sine die as I am
not convinced that the proposal to quadruple the payments is necessarily the
most appropriate resolution of the accumulations issue in this case. In the
mean time, direction will be given to the executor to provide up to date
valuations of the estate assets and their ability to earn income. Notice should
also be given to other parties who may have an interest in the outcome of this
application to give them an opportunity to intervene if they wish. In addition,
other issues in addition to the accumulations problem need to be considered.

ANALYSIS

[
30
]

Upon examination of the Statement of
Property and the financial statements already provided by the executor and the
instructions given in the will with regard to the management of the estate
assets it is quite probable that the rule against perpetuities, if it was still
the law of Saskatchewan, has been breached. I am of the view that the manner of
administering the estate assets to fulfil the charitable objects set out by the
testatrix in her will should be reviewed. Following are some of the questions
that come to mind. The list is not intended to be exhaustive.

[
31
]

For example, I am particularly concerned
that the executor is instructed to hold in trust the deceased’s “household and
personal effects” and is to only sell them at such time as the estate should
become depleted and finances are needed to continue the cash gift bequests.
What household and personal effects is the executor still in possession of? Is
the value of these assets appreciating or depreciating?

[
32
]

The will states that the deceased’s
farmland, being the SE and SW quarters of Section 27-5-14 W2, is “left to my
general estate” and that “monies from its rental shall be used for its
improvements of debts incurred by the farmland”. Thereafter moneys from the
rental are to be used to support the specific will bequests. The will also
empowers the executor to “manage, maintain, repair, and improve” the property,
to “carry on any business” and to be “reimbursed and remunerated for
undertaking such office.” While the financial reports filed by the executor to
date shows land rent of $5,700.00 in 2010-2011, the land rent in 2011-2012 is
only $2,000.00. The material filed by the executor to date does not indicate
whether there are buildings and improvements on the farm land which require
maintenance or which may become a burden on the estate in the future. I am of
the view that a decision should be made whether it is in the estate’s interest
to continue to hold title to farm land. To whom has the land been rented and on
what terms? Why not sell the land and place the money in secure, guaranteed
investments?

[
33
]

The estate also receives a significant
sum of money from royalties on the mineral holdings it owns and for surface
lease rentals on land it apparently no longer owns. Again, what is the current
market value of those mineral interests? Could these mineral interests not also
be liquidated so that the estate no longer bears the risk of depleting income?
Is it necessary that the executor be burdened with the obligation to continue
to supervise the administration of the mineral and surface leases?

[
34
]

On this application the named charities,
namely, the Weyburn Humane Society, the Weyburn Comprehensive School, and the executor as the person who decides who should receive the “underprivileged
student” scholarship, have all agreed to divide the surplus income
proportionately. Since the will provides for a gift of $6,000.00 per year for
the Humane Society and only $1,000.00 per year for scholarships to students, is
it necessarily fair and just that more than 85% of the surplus income should go
to the care of pets and less than 15% should go to deserving students?

[
35
]

The executor has indicated that the
estate will be paying an estimated $17,000.00 per year in income taxes. This is
because the estate is not a charitable institution but a testamentary trust.
The estate must file an income tax return each year and pay taxes on the
income. If the corpus of the estate was distributed to registered charitable
institutions to meet the objects of the gifts intended by the deceased, would
the monies otherwise payable in income tax not become available to the use of
those charitable objects, whether the Humane Society or the scholarships? Is
the estate also subject to a potential capital gain tax every 21 years under
current tax rules?

[
36
]

As regards the position taken by the
executor and apparently concurred in by the Humane Society and Weyburn
Comprehensive School that all of the income from this estate should remain with
them as the named beneficiaries and that no part should be paid to heirs or
next of kin of the deceased, I am of the view that this issue cannot be
definitively answered without a full and proper hearing with notice given to
any potential beneficiaries who might take on an intestacy and to the Public
Guardian and Trustee as required under
s. 49(3)
of
The
Trustee Act, 2009
.
While it is the case that the Last Will and Testament prescribes gifts to named
“charities” that presently exist or can be easily ascertained, it is also a
fact that the deceased specified the amount of the gift without providing for
any increase for inflation or any other reason. If the objects of the will can
be met, for example, by payment of a capital sum to the Weyburn Humane Society
and the Weyburn Comprehensive School which will meet the objects of the gift
forever into the future, could the balance of the estate not be paid to other
charitable institutions with similar objects under the
cy-pres
doctrine
(if not to the heirs or next of kin who might take under an intestacy in
respect to residue of the estate)?

DIRECTIONS

[
37
]

The answers to the above questions would
best be answered after a full and fair hearing with evidence tendered under
oath either by sworn affidavit or by the calling of witnesses to appear and
testify. I am further of the view that each of the parties named as
beneficiaries in the Last Will and Testament of Violet Delrose Moore should be
represented by separate counsel as their interests may be in conflict. More
specifically, the Weyburn Humane Society and the Weyburn Comprehensive School should each be represented by independent counsel. As is usually the case in proceedings
to resolve matters arising from the interpretation of a will, their costs would
be covered by the estate on a solicitor/client basis, as are the costs of the
solicitor acting for the executor.

[
38
]

Before any steps are taken to set this
matter down for a hearing, I will require the executor to hire professional
appraisers to establish the current fair market value of all of the estate
assets including household and personal effects (if any), the farm land, lots,
mineral rights, surface leases, the Glencarnham Royalty Trust #2, and the
interest in real property situate in the Province of Manitoba. There is no need
to obtain valuations of the Viterra shares or the bank accounts as those
valuations should be available by reference to available documentation. Such
valuations should be completed and filed with this Court within the next four
months. All appraisal costs will be paid by the estate.

[
39
]

In addition, I will require the executor
to make further inquiries regarding the existence of possible heirs or next of
kin to the deceased, Violet Delrose Moore. The executor may chose to hire a
professional genealogical research firm to assist him if he wishes. The results
of these inquiries must be filed within four months. In the event that possible
heirs or next of kin are located it is anticipated that the solicitor/client
costs of at least one representative of this class would also be paid by the
estate should he or she or they desire to participate.

[
40
]

A copy of this decision will be
delivered by the applicant to each of the Weyburn Comprehensive School Board
and to the Weyburn Humane Society so that they can consult their own solicitors
regarding their interests in this estate. Their solicitors should thereafter
file a Notice of Change of Representation in Form 2-40. A copy of the decision
should also be delivered to the office of the Public Guardian and Trustee so
that they will have advance notice of an invitation to participate in a hearing
pursuant to
s. 49(3)
of
The
Trustee Act, 2009
. If any next of kin are
identified, they also should receive a copy of this decision.

[
41
]

In the meantime, the executor shall file
updated financial statements in respect to

his administration of this estate to February 1,
2013, and for each six month interval thereafter. The executor shall also file
copies of any T3 Income and Trust Returns submitted to Revenue Canada to date, including Notices of Assessment or Re-assessment
.

[
42
]

After the asset appraisals have been
completed and the genealogical search for heirs or next of kin has been done, a
pre-trial conference can be arranged in the usual manner by counsel of record
to further define the issues to be resolved, the parties to be involved in a
hearing, who will have carriage of the action and who will bear the burden of
proof.

[
43
]

The executor shall have leave to apply
to this Court for further advice in regard to any matter that may arise in
connection with the implementation of these directions.

COSTS

[
44
]

The applicant, James Edward Kopec, as
executor of the Estate of Violet Delrose Moore, is entitled to recover his
solicitor/client costs of this application, to be taxed.
